column3: It exactly restates the Jahannam condition: neither death nor life, making the focus wording explicit.
God's giving and taking life grounds the divine power presupposed by the focus's exceptional punitive state.
Its denial of resurrection supplies a contrary premise to the focus's coming before the Lord for consequence.
It directly joins opposing God and His Messenger to enduring Jahannam, clarifying the focus's criminal outcome.
The next ayah supplies the contrasting arrival before God as a believing doer of good.
The general governance of life and death is already covered, but retains its cosmic framing.
It gives another direct formulation of disobedience ending in Jahannam forever.
The question to the Samiri does not add to the criminal's final condition.
God's ever-living, sustaining life contrasts with the focus's life deprived of life-giving benefit.
It associates worldly desire with Jahannam, but adds little beyond earlier punishment links.
The life-death-revival sequence supports return and judgment, though it repeats the divine-power route.
Hidden arrogance bears on culpability but does not specify the focus's final state.
It places idolatry under the Lord's accounting and denies success to disbelievers.
It completes the immediate contrast: eternal gardens reward the one who purifies himself.
It shows criminals visibly bound on the Day, adding a judgment-scene counterpart to their arrival.
It identifies fabrication and denial of signs as conduct for which criminals do not prosper.
Musa's request for Harun's support has no focused connection to the final punishment.
It gathers criminals at the trumpet blast, locating the focus's arrival within the resurrection scene.
It identifies Jahannam as the place denied by criminals, reinforcing the destination named in the focus.
The living status of those killed in God's way is a useful contrary form of life, but not the criminal state.
The sinners' admission of sins across deaths and lives adds a contrasting, unsuccessful desire for exit.
It directly disputes denial of resurrection and affirms God's binding promise to raise the dead.
Harun's defense in the calf episode does not clarify the focus.
Its objection to resurrection repeats the contrary premise already supplied by 23:37.
It directly states that criminals remain in Jahannam, though the permanence has already been established.
The doubled consequence across life and death is a secondary parallel to punishment spanning both states.
Dying in submission concerns faithful obligation, only distantly contrasting with arriving as a criminal.
The ever-living God who knows servants' sins supplies a divine contrast and basis for accountability.
The descent of the revelation is unrelated to the focus's judgment statement.
The staff becoming a moving serpent does not illuminate the criminal's final condition.
The name Yahya does not supply a relevant life-death or judgment relation here.
God's giving life, death, and final inheritance repeats the general authority route.
Dying in disbelief and receiving a curse gives a broad culpability parallel without the focus's condition.
Protected birth, death, and resurrection offer a distant positive contrast to the focus's deprivation.
Adam's disobedience in the garden is not a focused link to this punishment.
The challenge to wish for death concerns a claimed afterlife privilege rather than the focus's state.
It shows a manifest indecency receiving doubled punishment, adding a distinct accountability principle.
The lifelessness of false gods is a remote contrast, not an explanation of the criminal's condition.
The bare reference to criminals adds no new account of their fate.
It holds broad mercy together with an inescapable punishment for criminals, clarifying retributive finality.
Its living/dead contrast concerns hearing and response, only indirectly related to the focus wording.
The extraordinary restoration to life demonstrates power over death but is redundant here.
It makes a person bring acquired wrongdoing on the Day and receive an exact recompense.
The source of the Book does not explain the focus's criminal outcome.
The Samiri's worldly isolation and fixed appointment give only a remote, episode-specific punishment parallel.
It divides those present on the Day into wretched and happy, framing the focus's adverse end.
The cosmic alternation of living and dead repeats divine authority without adding judgment detail.
Death leads to return before the Knower, who informs people of what they did.
Concealed testimony is called sinful, but its legal instruction does not illuminate the final state.
It explicitly describes death followed by return to the Lord, the route assumed by coming before Him.
Death and later testimony are present, but the verse does not clarify the criminal's punishment.
It joins earthly life, death, and emergence from the earth, supporting resurrection after death.
Reviving the dead by God's permission illustrates divine power, but its miracle setting is secondary.
Its simple death-and-revival confession repeats the already established general pattern.
The debt-contract instructions do not add a focused relation to the ayah.
Return to God and His power over all things supply a concise foundation for the focus's judgment.
It contests a human claim over life and death, a secondary confirmation of divine authority.
Yusuf's deliverance from a plot does not bear on the final criminal condition.
The challenge to false deities' creative power is not a focused addition after earlier authority verses.
The attribution of death and life to God repeats the general authority already available.
God's bringing even hidden deeds forward supports accountability, but only generally.
The question about reviving the dead is another redundant statement of resurrection power.
The demonstration of revival adds a concrete image but little beyond the established resurrection route.
The gift of Yahya and response to Zakariyya do not clarify the focus.
The chosen servants and the polemic against partners are not a focused connection.
Inevitable death is a broad transition statement with limited added value here.
The description of the cow does not clarify the focus.
The question to the messengers has no relevant connection.
The saved speakers' freedom from further death forms a clear positive contrast to the focus's suspended state.
Reflection on the message does not develop the focus's final condition.
Worldly-life desire does not add a specific route to the focus after earlier punishment verses.
Universal mortality offers only a general contrast to the focus's non-death in Jahannam.
It extends the immediate righteous contrast by promising believers no injustice or deprivation.
Life, death, and final destination repeat the general authority-and-return route.
The earth containing living and dead is a distant spatial parallel to the focus's two states.
It gives a concrete grave crime whose recompense is abiding in Jahannam with great punishment.
Ibrahim's fulfillment is not a focused link to the criminal's end.
Its revival demonstration supports divine power but is redundant with several earlier resurrection examples.
It expands the focus precisely: no death is decreed for them and their Jahannam punishment is not eased.
Full recompense gives a concise rationale for the consequence stated in the focus.
The message entering criminal hearts distinguishes reception from response, but not their final state.
False divine claim receives Jahannam, adding a distinct offense-and-recompense formulation.
The mention of a sperm-drop does not add to the focus.
It depicts criminals being driven in a group to Jahannam, clarifying their arrival there.
It makes sin an acquisition borne by its doer, directly clarifying what it is to come as a criminal.
The believers' avoidance of associating partners does not add a focused relation.
It closes repentance at the arrival of death for persistent evildoers and assigns painful punishment.
Death comes from every direction without completion, closely explaining the focus's non-death under torment.
The adorned constellations do not illuminate the focus.
Investigating past criminals' outcomes gives a broad consequence pattern already well covered.
Divine guidance and vengeance provide only a general punitive frame.
The exclusion of deniers and arrogant criminals from paradise gives a distinct boundary to the focus's fate.
Repeated disbelief ending without forgiveness is relevant only as a broad antecedent to punishment.
The image of backbiting as eating dead flesh is not a focused account of the afterlife state.
Musa's private calling does not add to the criminal's final condition.
Persistent pride after distinct signs identifies a historical route into criminality.
Hypocrisy and distortion end in great afterlife punishment, but the connection is broad and redundant.
Unknown time and place of death offer no substantive explanation of the focus's Jahannam condition.
Calling the Quran a decisive word does not clarify the focus.
The wrongdoers' request for delay when punishment arrives reinforces the irreversibility of the warned outcome.
It states that those encompassed by their evil are companions of the Fire, abiding there forever.
It explicitly denies that the people of the Fire can ever emerge from it.
It repeats the wish to leave the Fire while decisively denying any exit.
It portrays the Fire as an enclosing bed and covering for wrongdoers, adding bodily enclosure to the focus's state.
It commands the arrogant to enter Jahannam and remain there, joining culpability, entry, and permanence.
It describes the Fire's enclosing walls and its inescapable, punishing provision.
It gathers devils with those who rebelled and brings them around Jahannam, extending the focus's arrival scene.
It makes coming to Hell universal before deliverance, sharpening the distinct criminal outcome of the focus.
It depicts garments of fire, boiling liquid, and iron maces for those who dispute about their Lord.
It shows that every attempted escape from anguish results in being returned to the Fire.
It calls those with light scales the losers abiding in Jahannam.
The condemned acknowledge that wretchedness overcame them, giving voice to the criminal condition.
Bound in a narrow place in the Fire, they call for death, directly paralleling the focus's denied release.
It answers their call by denying a single death and directing them to call for many deaths.
Whenever the defiantly disobedient try to leave the Fire, they are returned to it.
It depicts chains placed on the disbelievers' necks, adding a judgmental form of restraint.
It identifies Jahannam as the promised destination for those who disbelieved.
It depicts the disbelievers being driven in groups to Jahannam, closely complementing coming before the Lord as criminals.
It places Pharaoh's people before the Fire repeatedly and then in the severest punishment on the Hour.
It names the Fire as the lasting recompense of God's enemies.
The inhabitants ask Malik for their Lord to end them, and the reply leaves them remaining there.
It begins the detailed torment scene with the tree of Zaqqum as the food of the sinful.
The address to Jahannam foregrounds its capacity to receive the condemned on that Day.
It depicts the condemned being driven forcefully toward the Fire of Jahannam.
Their faces are dragged into the Fire while they are told to taste its touch.
It identifies the disbelieving, astray group as the contrasting final class.
It gives that class a burning in the Blaze as its final outcome.
It assigns the punishment of Jahannam to those who disbelieve in their Lord.
Its raging sound and boiling agitation convey the active severity of that destination.
It commands that the condemned person be seized and burned in Hell.
It continues the command by directing him into the blazing Fire.
The seventy-cubit chain adds an enduring physical image of restraint in punishment.
It announces that the criminal will be made to burn in Saqar.
It describes Saqar as a scorching, visible force upon human bodies.
It names Jahannam as a place lying in wait for the transgressors.
It says the transgressors remain in it for ages, directly adding duration.
It denies them coolness and any drink there, intensifying the focus's life-without-relief condition.
It states that they will burn in the Hellfire.
It gives a burning Fire as the place reached by the wretched faces.
The drink from a searing spring adds a distinct deprivation within that punishment.
It casts the hoarder into the Crushing Fire, linking acquired wrongdoing to a consuming end.
It identifies that Fire as God's kindled fire.
It describes the Fire as closed over them, reinforcing the absence of escape.
It identifies the abyss as the final home of the light-scaled person.
It explains that abyss as a blazing Fire.
It states that disbelievers are companions of the Fire, abiding there forever.
